title: Handshake hiccups — late-night debug scratchpad
content:
Goal: quick, messy notes to reproduce and isolate intermittent 401 then 429 pattern observed on a handful of customer requests. Keep timeline, commands tried, and hypotheses.

Summary of observed behaviour:
- Client A (mobile SDK) occasionally sees a 401, immediately followed by multiple 429s for the same API key. Happens in bursts: 1–3 users every ~10–30 minutes.
- Timing: often around minute boundaries (xx:00–xx:02) but not exclusively.
- When key is rotated server-side, incidence drops for ~30–90 minutes, then returns.
- Rate limit headers inconsistent: sometimes X-RateLimit-Remaining present, other times missing.

Minimal repro steps I ran locally:
1) simple curl to hosted api using known API key (api-key-redacted):
   curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer api-key-redacted" \ 
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ 
        -d '{"input":"hello"}' \ 
        https://api.redwoodai.example/v1/generate

   Observed: usually 200; reproduced 401 once at 2024-10-17T23:11:14Z. Response body: "{\"error\":\"Unauthorized\",\"message\":\"invalid_api_key\"}"
   Response headers (when 401 happened):
     HTTP/2 401
     date: Thu, 17 Oct 2024 23:11:14 GMT
     content-type: application/json
     x-request-id: req_7f4c1e
     x-service-region: us-west-2
   No rate-limit headers included with that 401.

2) Immediately re-sent same curl (same key) 4 times in <5s:
   - First repeat => 429 with body: "{\"error\":\"Too Many Requests\",\"retry_after\":2}"
   - Headers on 429 responses (sample):
       x-ratelimit-limit: 600
       x-ratelimit-remaining: 0
       x-ratelimit-reset: 1697616700
       retry-after: 2
   - reset value corresponds to epoch 2024-10-17T23:11:40Z (approx).

3) Tried short Python script that does naive retry-on-401 then exponential backoff:
   import requests, time
   for i in range(8):
       r = requests.post(url, headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {API_KEY}'}, json={'input':'x'})
       print(i, r.status_code, r.text)
       if r.status_code == 401:
           time.sleep(0.5)
           continue
       if r.status_code == 429:
           time.sleep(min(60, (2**i)))
           continue

   Result: script saw 401 then ~3x 429s then resumed normal 200s.

Raw snippets from server logs (scrubbed request ids):
- [2024-10-17T23:11:13Z] key=usr_abc123 auth=fail reason=signature-mismatch?
- [2024-10-17T23:11:14Z] key=usr_abc123 code=401 message=invalid_api_key client_ip=203.0.113.4
- [2024-10-17T23:11:15Z] key=usr_abc123 code=429 message=rate_limit_exceeded limit=600 remaining=0 reset=1697616700

Notes on what I have ruled out so far:
- Not client clock drift on our end: system times checked, JWTs issued by client are not used by this flow.
- Not simple per-ip WAF blocking: same behaviour seen from multiple client IPs including home/office.
- Not immediate token expiry: tokens in this flow are long-lived API keys, TTL >> incidents.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Short-lived internal quota checkpoint: an auth microservice occasionally flags a key as invalid for a few seconds (intermittent DB hiccup or replication lag), which triggers 401. The proxy layer then applies stricter rate limiting when seeing repeated auth fails for same key, leading to follow-up 429s.
2) Race between key rotation and active requests: if a key is marked rotated in metadata store, first request after rotation fails 401 and throttler considers the key as newly flagged and throttles aggressively.
3) Downstream caching bug: auth cache TTL is very small; cache miss + heavy DB read causes a temporary drop in allowed tokens leading to a local counter miscalc (remaining => 0).
4) Upstream throttling enforcement shift: tokens with previous soft-allowance get bumped into hard-limit due to cluster-wide recalculation on minute boundaries. Explains clustering at minute boundaries.

Experiments to run next (short):
- Add detailed logging on auth service for key state transitions (valid -> flagged -> rotated) with timestamps (ns) and origin of change (api, admin, rotation job).
- Reproduce with synthetic spike: use 10 parallel clients hitting same key across 2 regions to see distribution. Observe if 401s appear on single node or cluster-wide.
- Force a controlled rotation and observe timeline (rotate key at T0, watch for 401/429 pattern) — compare to uncontrolled incidents.
- Temporary patch: suppress aggressive throttling for keys that returned 401 within last 10s (treat auth failure as transient) — watch false positives.

Longer-form experiments / telemetry to collect:
- Correlate x-request-id across auth service logs, gateway, and rate-limiter to see sequence of events.
- Add a metric: auth_fail_then_rate_limit_count per key per minute.
- Track replication lag of key metadata tables around incidents (DB metrics).

Quick mitigation (for ops):
- If customer hits many 401->429 incidents, allow single-use manual override by rotating the key (customer sees improvement historically). But this is a bandaid, not fix.
- Increase backoff defaults in mobile SDK to jittered exponential with base 1s and cap 16s; avoid hammering after 401.

Questions / unknowns:
- Does the gateway enforce any extra policy on a key after an auth failure? I need someone from gateway team to confirm whether a 401 triggers sticky throttle.
- Are there any cron jobs that re-evaluate quota buckets at minute boundaries that might coincidentally zero out remaining counts?

Notes-to-self / todo:
- @Noah add a logging flag to auth service (verbose=true) for 24h window starting 2024-10-18T08:00Z.
- @Priya run synthetic parallel test from us-west-2 and eu-west-1 next Tue 10/22 (script below).

Synthetic script (one-liner; run from two shells):
for i in {1..200}; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "Authorization: Bearer api-key-redacted" \ 
  -d '{"input":"poke"}' https://api.redwoodai.example/v1/generate & done; wait

If we see: mostly 200 then cluster of 401+429 from different clients -> strong sign of cluster-side state change.

Edge-case thoughts:
- If there's a service mesh sidecar doing local caching of key information, maybe sidecar crash + restart causes short gap where endpoint rejects keys until it fetches state. That would create bursts around restart times. Check pod restart counts.
- If a rotation job marks key as revoked and then unrevoked by mistake (race), we'd see revive after rotation. Check rotation job history.

Last quick log excerpts for timeline clustering (personal, messy):
- 23:09:55 -> normal 200s
- 23:11:13 -> first 401 blast (single request)
- 23:11:13.5 -> 429 flood (3–5 requests)
- 23:11:41 -> back to 200s
- 23:40:02 -> small 401 spike again (two requests)

Closing note: this doc is my working scratchpad. Keep it messy. The target next step is to get gateway and auth service owners to enable a trace + find the earliest point where state goes from valid -> invalid for the key.

Appendix: small checklist for post-mortem meeting
- capture traces for one incident window (raw logs + metrics)
- reproduce in staging with controlled rotation and cache eviction
- validate gateway behavior on auth-failure -> throttle mappings
- propose short-term SDK backoff change and ops mitigation runbook

-- A.P.
